The wedding in Ludhiana had one generator, and it died at eight, in the middle of the mehndi, just as the rain came down on the tent. In the dark, Kavitha, twenty, heard her Baljeet Bua say to another aunty, "London girl. Can't even sit cross-legged. Too English." Kavitha's throat tightened. A week ago in Leeds, a lecturer had asked her where she was "originally" from, even though she was born three streets from the university.
When the lights came back, she had henna drying on both palms and nowhere to hide her face. She took a breath, walked over and sat, carefully, on the floor next to Bua. "My knees are English," she said, "but my Punjabi is fine, Bua. You taught me the tappe yourself." Bua laughed, surprised. Kavitha sang one. Some aunties joined in. She didn't apologise for her accent.

qa.a: At eight, in the middle of the mehndi.

qa.a: She sat by Bua, owned her English knees and her Punjabi with humour, and sang a tappa without apologising for her accent.

qa.a: Bua seemed surprised and pleased, perhaps realising Kavitha carried more of the family culture than she had assumed.

On her first week at the Delhi college, Seema, nineteen, was introduced to her classmates as "the Dubai girl". They teased her Hindi, which had Arabic words tumbling into it. "Say it again, 'khalas'!" In Dubai, where she was born, her school friends had always called her "the Indian one". Now, at the canteen, a girl said, "You're not proper Indian, na? You don't even know the festivals." Seema went red. She knew Eid and Diwali and National Day. That evening she sat on the metro, staring at her reflection, wondering what she was.
Her friend Jasleen, who had grown up in Canada before moving back, sat with her at lunch the next day. "They call me 'Canada' too. So what? We're both." When the girl teased her again, Seema said, lightly, "I'm Indian and I'm from Dubai. I get two sets of sweets." People laughed with her.

passage: Last winter in Kolkata, my cousin Anirban watched me eat fish with a fork and said, "Uday, you've become a full saheb." Everyone laughed. My Pishi added that my Bangla sounded like a tourist's. I laughed along, then went up to the terrace and felt about ten centimetres tall. Two weeks later, back at uni in Sydney, a classmate asked why I'd brought "that smelly curry" to a group lunch and whether I'd go back home after my degree. I've been home my whole life, I wanted to say. It took me months to stop shrinking in both places. Now when Anirban teases me, I tell him I'm the only one in the family who can make shorshe ilish and a decent pavlova. And at uni I bring the fish curry anyway. Both are mine. Nobody gets to hand out permission for the mix I am.

qa.a: Anirban said, "Uday, you've become a full saheb."
